subject: Civil Engineering
title: Speed Design and the Design Vehicle
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Speed Design and the Design Vehicle.

hook.text: A road designed for sports cars fails when an 18-wheeler tries to make the turn.

buildup.text: The design vehicle is the largest vehicle the road must safely accommodate.

discovery.text: Turn radii, lane widths, and clearances are all sized to the design vehicle.

twist.text: Design speed is the maximum safe speed — it governs curve radii and sight distance.

climax.text: Interstate highways design for semi-trucks at 70 mph — every dimension follows from that.

punchline.text: Design for the biggest vehicle at the target speed. Everything else follows.

quiz.question: Why do engineers use a 'design vehicle' in road design?
options: To determine how many vehicles the road can handle daily
To ensure the road safely accommodates the largest expected vehicle
To set the speed limit for the entire road segment

details.summary: Design speed is the maximum safe speed for a specific road section that determines all geometric features including curve radius, sight distance, and lane width.
details.whyItMatters: Choosing the right design speed and design vehicle prevents both under-building, which creates safety hazards, and over-building, which wastes money and land on unnecessarily wide roads.
takeaways: Design speed determines minimum curve radius and sight distance requirements
The WB-67 design vehicle represents the largest common semi-trailer truck
Intersection turn radii must accommodate the design vehicle's turning path

faq.question: How is design speed different from the posted speed limit?
faq.answer: Design speed is the engineering standard used to set geometric features and is usually higher than the posted limit to provide a safety margin. A road designed for 110 km/h might have an 80 km/h speed limit. The geometry should safely accommodate occasional speeds above the limit.

faq.question: Why does the choice of design vehicle matter so much?
faq.answer: If intersection corners are too tight for trucks, they mount curbs and damage infrastructure. If lanes are too narrow, large vehicles encroach on adjacent lanes. Using an oversized design vehicle wastes space, while undersizing creates safety hazards and maintenance costs.
